changes.before: Noise is unwanted variation in the signal. It can come from movement, electrical interference, heart activity, muscle activity, electrode instability, or unrelated neural activity. Signal-to-noise ratio asks how much useful signal exists compared with unwanted activity.
changes.after: A useful signal depends on the question being asked. Movement, muscle activity, electrical interference and electrode instability can contaminate a recording. An artifact correlated with task labels may look predictive during training. Compare raw traces, reference channels, timing and recording conditions before interpreting a detected event. A numerical threshold is only one observation.

changes.before: If a large deflection appears on many electrodes exactly with the ECG heartbeat, it is more likely cardiac artifact than a single neuron.
changes.after: Synthetic lab example: deflections recur roughly once per second and align with an ECG reference on several channels. This raises suspicion of cardiac contamination. Flag the segment and inspect synchronized traces and acquisition settings before deciding how to exclude or process it; do not infer a neuron identity or recommend a patient intervention.

changes.before: A neural recording is not one number. It is a sequence: sample 1, sample 2, sample 3, each tied to a time point. Voltage changes mean different things depending on when they happen and how they relate to nearby samples. Two kinds of activity live in these traces: sharp, brief dips or blips lasting a millisecond or two — spikes, the action potentials of individual neurons near the electrode — and slower, rolling waves that ride underneath them, the local field potential (LFP), which is the summed activity of thousands of neurons in the neighborhood. Same wire, two signals at different timescales. In toy BCI code, all of it usually becomes a list or array of values.
changes.after: A time series needs ordered measurements, units and timing. For equally spaced samples, time at index i is start time + i / sampling rate. A list alone does not tell us the sampling rate. Intracellular membrane voltage and extracellular electrode voltage are different measurements; do not transfer their thresholds or amplitudes between recordings. Extracellular signals can be processed to study rapid events or slower field activity. Detecting an event does not by itself identify a neuron.

changes.before: If samples are [-70, -68, -45, -42, -70] mV, the middle values only look spike-like because they rise sharply relative to the surrounding samples.
changes.after: Synthetic membrane-voltage example: [-70, -68, -45, -42, -70] mV, sampled at 1,000 samples/second starting at 0 seconds. Index 2 occurs at 2/1,000 = 0.002 seconds. The first-to-last timestamp span is 4 milliseconds. This short toy list is not a validated spike recording.

changes.before: Firing rate means spikes per unit time. A decoder often cares less about every exact spike time and more about whether a neuron is firing more or less during a movement or intention window.
changes.after: For a specified observation window, mean firing rate is spike count divided by duration in seconds. If the events are only threshold candidates, call the result a threshold-event rate. A rate discards exact event timing. Longer windows pool more observations but can hide rapid changes; shorter windows can fluctuate strongly. Neither choice is universally best for a decoder.

changes.before: Spike detection is a gate. Set the gate too low and noise walks in; set it too high and real spikes get locked out.
changes.after: Count entries through a gate, not every moment spent beyond the gate. A more permissive threshold can admit more unwanted events. Which numerical direction is permissive depends on detection polarity.

changes.before: A spike detector usually checks whether a waveform crosses a threshold and has a plausible shape. The hard part is not writing `if voltage > threshold`; it is choosing a threshold that separates neural events from noise and artifact.
changes.after: A positive-threshold event starts when a sample reaches or exceeds a chosen level after the previous sample was below it. Consecutive above-threshold samples belong to one continuous episode in this toy detector. We assume the trace starts below threshold; an above-threshold first sample is counted as one episode by convention. Real detection also needs recording context, waveform checks and handling of artifacts and repeated detections. An event is not automatically a physiological spike or an identified neuron.

changes.before: With threshold -50 mV, samples [-70, -62, -48, -44, -69] include a threshold crossing. If noise also reaches -49 mV, code needs more evidence than threshold alone.
changes.after: Synthetic membrane-voltage samples [-70, -55, -42, -66, -44, -39, -71] mV contain three samples at or above -50 mV, but only two above-threshold episodes. At -40 mV only the -39 sample qualifies, so the episode count is one. These are toy threshold events, not confirmed spikes.

changes.before: Filtering keeps some frequency ranges and suppresses others. Smoothing reduces rapid jumps by averaging nearby samples. Both are preprocessing steps, and both can help or hurt depending on the feature you need.
changes.after: A filter transforms a signal. A centered three-sample moving average replaces a middle value with the average of itself and its two neighbors. It changes genuine events as well as unwanted variation. Here we output only centers with all three neighbors available, so a list of N samples produces N-2 values. Boundary handling and timing conventions belong in the method description.

changes.before: A moving average may make an LFP trend easier to see, but it can smear the exact timing of a narrow spike.
changes.after: For synthetic values [10, 12, 50, 13, 11], the full-window centered averages are [24, 25, 24.6667]. The middle output is (12 + 50 + 13) / 3 = 25. A real narrow peak would also be reduced; a smoother plot is not evidence that only noise was removed.

changes.before: Loops: Count Spikes in a Trace
changes.after: Loops: Count Threshold Episodes

changes.before:
signal_mv = [-70, -55, -42, -66, -44, -39, -71]
threshold_mv = -45
spike_count = 0

for sample in signal_mv:
    if sample >= threshold_mv:
        spike_count = spike_count + 1

print("Spikes:", spike_count)
changes.after:
def count_events(samples, threshold):
    count = 0
    previous_above = False
    for sample in samples:
        above = sample >= threshold
        if above and not previous_above:
            count += 1
        previous_above = above
    return count

trace = [-70, -55, -42, -66, -44, -39, -71]
print("Events:", count_events(trace, -50))

changes.before: Every BCI begins by sampling neural activity over time. Code cannot detect spikes, smooth noise, or decode intent until the signal is represented as ordered samples.
changes.after: Neurons receive and transmit signals through electrical and chemical processes. A membrane voltage is measured across the cell membrane; an extracellular electrode measures voltage outside cells. Before calculating features, identify what was measured and how each sample maps to time.
